_comment: Single source of truth. Feeds BOTH the private posting kit (tools/posting-kit) and the public answer pages (public/gaby/quiz/<slug>/). Run: npm run quiz:build. Every quiz needs: day, slug, situation, situationEn, place, question, options[], answer, why (may contain <b>/<i>), takeaway. The slug is the public URL and lives forever in social comments — never change one after posting, and never let it give the answer away.

quizzes.question: You are at the bar and want to ask what tapas they have. Which one is right?
quizzes.why: You are asking the bar, not one person — so it is tienen, the ustedes form. ¿Qué tapas tiene? is grammatical but it asks a single individual, which is not how you address staff behind a counter. And qué takes the accent in a question.
quizzes.takeaway: Addressing a business is almost always plural in Spain.

quizzes.question: You want the set lunch. You say “Sí, el del día, por favor.” What is missing?
quizzes.answer: menú — “Sí, el menú del día, por favor.”
quizzes.why: English lets you drop the noun once it is obvious. Spanish wants it in there: el menú del día is a fixed phrase, and leaving out menú makes el del día sound like you are pointing at something unnamed.
quizzes.takeaway: You will be understood without it. You will also sound like you are guessing.

quizzes.question: You want to ask if they know where the nearest health centre is. Saber or conocer?
options: ¿Conoce dónde está el centro de salud?
¿Sabe dónde está el centro de salud?
quizzes.answer: ¿Sabe dónde está el centro de salud?
quizzes.why: Saber is for facts and information — an address, a time, how to do something. Conocer is for being familiar with a person or a place. You want the fact, so it is sabe. You would use conocer in ¿Conoce este barrio?
quizzes.takeaway: Saber = information. Conocer = familiarity.

quizzes.place: the queue at your local ayuntamiento
quizzes.question: You turn up at the town hall to register. The first thing they ask is whether you have one of these. Which?
quizzes.why: Cita previa — a prior appointment — is the phrase that runs Spanish bureaucracy, and almost nothing happens without one. Cita is feminine, so it is una and previa. Anterior means previous in time (the previous one), not booked in advance.
quizzes.takeaway: Learn “cita previa” before you learn anything else. You will need it for the NIE, the padrón and the doctor.

quizzes.question: The officer asks “¿Cuál es el motivo de su viaje?” You are moving here. What do you say?
quizzes.answer: Both are fine — “Vengo a vivir aquí” is what you will hear most.
quizzes.why: After a verb of motion, Spanish uses a + infinitive to give the purpose: vengo a vivir, voy a comprar. Para + infinitive is also correct and slightly more emphatic about the goal. What does not work is leaving the preposition out.
quizzes.takeaway: Verb of motion + a + infinitive. “Vengo a…”, “Voy a…”, “Salgo a…”.

quizzes.place: the taxi rank outside the terminal
quizzes.question: You get in and want to give the driver an address. Which opener sounds native?
quizzes.why: Llevar is to take someone somewhere, and it is the verb for taxis and lifts. Tomar is what you do to a bus or a coffee, not to a passenger. Conducir is to drive the vehicle itself, which is his job, not your request.
quizzes.takeaway: You llevar a person. You tomar a bus. The driver conduce.

quizzes.place: a bank branch on a Tuesday morning
quizzes.question: You want an everyday current account. What do you ask for?
quizzes.why: Cuenta corriente is the fixed term for a current account. Actual is a false friend — it means current in time (present-day), not current as in an account, so cuenta actual reads as “my present account”.
quizzes.takeaway: Actual = present-day, not “actual”. One of the false friends that bites hardest.

quizzes.place: a phone shop on the high street
quizzes.question: You do not want to be locked in. How do you ask for a contract with no minimum term?
quizzes.why: Permanencia is the industry word for the lock-in period, and sin permanencia is printed on every advert. Sin contrato means prepaid, which is a different product, and sin duración is not a thing.
quizzes.takeaway: Sin permanencia = no lock-in. Sin contrato = prepaid. They are not the same offer.

quizzes.question: You have a headache and need to say so. Which is right?
quizzes.why: Doler works like gustar: the body part is the subject and you are the indirect object — literally “the head hurts to me”. So it is me duele la cabeza, and with plurals me duelen las piernas. You can also say tengo dolor de cabeza.
quizzes.takeaway: Me duele + singular. Me duelen + plural. Never “estoy dolor”.

quizzes.place: an empty flat with the estate agent waiting
quizzes.question: The agent mentions the deposit you will have to put down. Which word is that?
quizzes.why: La fianza is the rental deposit, normally one or two months. El aval is a separate and much bigger thing — a guarantee, often several months held in a bank, which landlords ask of newcomers with no Spanish payslips. Depósito exists but is not the rental term.
quizzes.takeaway: Fianza = deposit. Aval = guarantee. Ask which one they want before you sign.

quizzes.question: You are thanking a neighbour for their help. Which one?
quizzes.why: Por covers the cause or reason — what you are grateful because of. Para covers the destination or purpose: Esto es para ti. Thanks is always por: por la ayuda, por venir, por todo.
quizzes.takeaway: Por = the reason behind. Para = the goal ahead.

quizzes.place: a friend’s kitchen, making small talk
quizzes.question: You want to say you are bored right now. Which?
quizzes.why: Estar is the state you are in now, so estoy aburrido = I am bored. Ser is what you are as a rule, so soy aburrido tells the room you are a boring person. The same trap hits listo (ready vs clever) and rico (tasty vs wealthy).
quizzes.takeaway: Estoy aburrido = I am bored. Soy aburrido = I am boring. Pick carefully.

quizzes.place: a shop, having just knocked something over
quizzes.question: You did something clumsy and want to say you are embarrassed. Which?
quizzes.why: Embarazada means pregnant. To say embarrassed, Spanish uses me da vergüenza (it gives me embarrassment) or qué vergüenza. This is the single most reliable way for an English speaker to derail a conversation in Spain.
quizzes.takeaway: Embarazada = pregnant. Vergüenza = embarrassment.

quizzes.question: You have a blocked nose and a sore throat. What do you tell the pharmacist?
quizzes.answer: Estoy constipado. (constipada if you are female)
quizzes.why: Constipado means having a cold — nothing to do with the English word. The pharmacist will hand you something for your nose. Note it takes estar, because it is a temporary state, and it agrees with you: constipado / constipada.
quizzes.takeaway: Estoy constipado = I have a cold. It is not what it looks like.

quizzes.place: a government office with a queue number
quizzes.question: Same afternoon, two places. Where would you use usted?
quizzes.why: Spain is far more tú than most learners expect. In bars, shops and among anyone near your age, tú is normal and usted can sound stiff or distancing. Keep usted for officials, much older strangers, and formal paperwork — and drop it the moment they tutean you.
quizzes.takeaway: Default to tú in daily life. Save usted for the counter with a queue number.

quizzes.place: a bar terrace with two friends
quizzes.question: You are addressing two friends informally, in Spain. Which?
quizzes.why: Spain keeps vosotros for informal plural you, with its own endings — queréis, tenéis, sois. Latin America dropped it and uses ustedes for everyone. If you learned Spanish in the Americas, this is the form you have to add.
quizzes.takeaway: In Spain, vosotros for friends, ustedes for formality. Both exist.

quizzes.place: a bar, at the counter rather than a table
quizzes.question: You want a small draught beer. What do Spaniards actually say?
quizzes.why: ¿Me pones…? — literally “will you put me…?” — is the standard, friendly way to order at a bar in Spain. Quiero is not rude but lands flat, and deseo belongs in a letter from 1950. Me pone is the usted version.
quizzes.takeaway: ¿Me pones…? at the bar. ¿Me pone…? if you are being formal.

quizzes.place: a restaurant, at the end of a long lunch
quizzes.question: You want the bill. Which is the natural one?
quizzes.why: Cobrar is to charge, and ¿nos cobras? is how it is usually done, often with cuando puedas to stay polite. La cuenta, por favor is also perfectly fine. A factura is a formal invoice for a business, and a recibo is the little slip afterwards.
quizzes.takeaway: La cuenta = the bill. La factura = the invoice you claim on.

quizzes.place: a queue, filling in a form
quizzes.question: Someone asks for your address. Which question did they use?
quizzes.why: Before the verb ser, Spanish picks cuál when it is asking you to select a specific piece of information: ¿Cuál es tu nombre?, ¿Cuál es el problema?. Qué + ser asks for a definition — ¿Qué es una fianza? means “what is a fianza?”.
quizzes.takeaway: Cuál asks which one. Qué asks what a thing means.

quizzes.question: It is 40 degrees. How do you say it is very hot?
quizzes.why: Calor is a noun — it is heat, not hot — and nouns take mucho, not muy. Muy only modifies adjectives and adverbs: muy caluroso, muy rápido. The weather uses hacer: hace frío, hace viento, hace sol.
quizzes.takeaway: Muy + adjective. Mucho + noun. Hace + weather.

quizzes.situationEn: A verb that changes by country
quizzes.question: In Spain, how do you say you are going to catch the bus?
quizzes.answer: Both work in Spain — coger is the everyday one.
quizzes.why: Coger is completely ordinary in Spain for catching, taking or picking something up. In much of Latin America the same verb is vulgar, which is why many courses avoid teaching it — but in Madrid you will hear it constantly. Tomar is also fine and travels better.
quizzes.takeaway: In Spain: coger. Across the Atlantic: tomar. Know why they differ.

quizzes.place: the market, with a queue behind you
quizzes.question: You want half a kilo of tomatoes. Which?
options: ¿Me pone la mitad de kilo de tomates?
¿Me pone medio de kilo de tomates?
quizzes.why: Medio goes straight in front of the unit with no article and no de: medio kilo, media hora, medio litro. La mitad is the half of a specific thing — la mitad del pan, half of the loaf — which is a different idea.
quizzes.takeaway: Medio kilo, media hora. La mitad de = half of that particular thing.

quizzes.question: They ask “¿Cómo lo quiere?” You want a little off, just the ends. Which?
quizzes.why: Las puntas are the ends of the hair, and this is the phrase that saves haircuts. Useful neighbours: por detrás (at the back), por los lados (at the sides), las patillas (sideburns), and no muy corto (not too short).
quizzes.takeaway: Las puntas, por detrás, por los lados. Three phrases, one survivable haircut.

quizzes.question: A neighbour steps into the lift. What do you say?
quizzes.why: Greeting people in shared spaces is close to obligatory in Spain — the lift, the stairwell, a small shop, a doctor's waiting room. Saying nothing reads as rude rather than private. Buenos días until about 2pm, then buenas tardes; hola, buenas works all day.
quizzes.takeaway: Say hello when you walk into a small space. Silence is the impolite option.

quizzes.place: a tapas bar, ordering for the table
quizzes.question: You like tapas — plural. Which?
quizzes.why: Gustar does not mean “to like”, it means to be pleasing. The thing you like is the subject, so it drives the verb: me gusta el café (singular) but me gustan las tapas (plural). Yo gusto says that you are the one being pleasing.
quizzes.takeaway: The thing you like is the subject. Count it, then pick gusta or gustan.

quizzes.situationEn: A word that traps English speakers
quizzes.place: your new town, describing it to someone back home
quizzes.question: You want to say the people here are very friendly. Which?
options: La gente aquí son muy amables.
La gente aquí es muy amable.
Las gentes aquí son muy amables.
quizzes.answer: La gente aquí es muy amable.
quizzes.why: Gente is a singular feminine collective noun in Spanish, even though it means many people. So the verb is singular — es — and the adjective is singular too: amable. Las gentes exists but is literary and will sound odd in conversation.
quizzes.takeaway: La gente es. Not son. One of the last errors to disappear.

quizzes.question: You want your coffee to take away. Which?
quizzes.why: Para llevar is the fixed phrase for takeaway, and the opposite is para tomar aquí (to have here) — which is the question you will be asked first. Para salir means in order to go out, which will get you a puzzled look.
quizzes.takeaway: ¿Para tomar aquí o para llevar? Learn the question, not just the answer.

quizzes.situationEn: A noun that looks like it broke
quizzes.place: a bar, ordering the simplest thing there is
quizzes.question: You want cold water. Which is correct?
quizzes.why: Agua is feminine, but a singular feminine noun starting with a stressed a- takes el instead of la, purely so the two a-sounds do not collide. The noun stays feminine, so the adjective does too: el agua fría. In the plural it goes back to normal: las aguas.
quizzes.takeaway: El agua, but fría. The article changes; the gender does not.

quizzes.place: a bar, meeting someone for the first time
quizzes.question: You have lived here two months. Which?
options: Hace dos meses que vivo aquí.
Hace dos meses que viví aquí.
quizzes.answer: Hace dos meses que vivo aquí.
quizzes.why: For something that started in the past and is still going, Spanish uses hace + time + que + present tense. The present tense is the part English speakers drop, because English says “I have lived”. Por dos meses suggests a fixed stint that is over or planned to end.
quizzes.takeaway: Hace dos meses que vivo aquí. Present tense, because you still live here.

quizzes.place: the doorway after your language class
quizzes.question: You want to suggest meeting a friend on Friday. Which?
quizzes.why: Quedar is the everyday verb for arranging to meet socially — ¿quedamos?, he quedado con Ana. Encontrarse leans towards running into someone by chance, and reunirse is a meeting with an agenda. Quedar is also how you say something suits you: me queda bien.
quizzes.takeaway: Quedar = meet up on purpose. Encontrarse = bump into. Reunirse = at work.

quizzes.place: a café, trying to explain your job
quizzes.question: English "conversation" becomes which Spanish word?
quizzes.why: English -tion becomes -ción, and every one of them is feminine: la conversación, la información, la nación. The accent is not optional — it marks the stress on the last syllable.
quizzes.takeaway: -tion → -ción, always feminine, always accented.

quizzes.question: English "university" becomes which Spanish word?
quizzes.why: English -ty becomes -dad (or -tad): ciudad, libertad, dificultad. They are all feminine, and unlike -ción they carry no written accent, because they already end in a consonant that takes the stress naturally.
quizzes.takeaway: -ty → -dad. Feminine, and no accent needed.

quizzes.question: How do you turn "rápido" into "rapidly"?
quizzes.why: Add -mente to the feminine form of the adjective: rápida → rápidamente, lenta → lentamente. The original accent stays where it was, even though the word grows.
quizzes.takeaway: Feminine adjective + -mente. Keep the accent you started with.

quizzes.question: English "delicious" becomes which Spanish word?
quizzes.why: English -ous becomes -oso: famoso, curioso, nervioso, generoso. It is an adjective, so it agrees: una comida deliciosa.
quizzes.takeaway: -ous → -oso. Then make it agree with what it describes.

quizzes.question: English "document" becomes which Spanish word?
quizzes.why: English -ment usually becomes -mento: momento, argumento, departamento. Watch the exception you will need most: government is gobierno, not gobiernamento.
quizzes.takeaway: -ment → -mento. Except gobierno, which you will meet at the town hall.

quizzes.question: English "difference" becomes which Spanish word?
quizzes.why: English -ence/-ance becomes -encia/-ancia: importancia, experiencia, paciencia. All feminine. Note Spanish spells it with one r — diferencia, not differencia.
quizzes.takeaway: -ence → -encia, feminine. Spanish rarely doubles consonants.

quizzes.question: Your dentist is a woman. What do you call her?
quizzes.why: -ist becomes -ista, and the word does not change for gender — only the article does: el dentista / la dentista, el artista / la artista. There is no dentisto.
quizzes.takeaway: -ista never changes. Change the article instead.

quizzes.place: reading a sign on a public building
quizzes.question: English "public" becomes which Spanish word?
quizzes.why: English -ic becomes -ico, and the stress lands two syllables from the end, so it takes a written accent: público, música, práctico. Careful — publicó with the accent at the end means “he published”.
quizzes.takeaway: -ic → -ico, accented on the third-from-last syllable.

quizzes.question: English "active" becomes which Spanish word?
quizzes.why: English -ive becomes -ivo: positivo, creativo, intensivo. Adjective, so it agrees: una persona activa.
quizzes.takeaway: -ive → -ivo, then agree it.

quizzes.place: a bank, reading the small print
quizzes.question: English "necessary" becomes which Spanish word?
quizzes.why: English -ary becomes -ario: ordinario, voluntario, salario. The trap in necesario is the spelling: English doubles the c and the s, Spanish doubles neither.
quizzes.takeaway: -ary → -ario. And Spanish almost never doubles a consonant.

quizzes.place: a theatre, looking for the way out
quizzes.question: You see a sign saying "ÉXITO". What does it mean?
quizzes.why: Éxito means success — tuvo mucho éxito, it was a big hit. The way out is la salida, which is what every emergency sign in Spain actually says.
quizzes.takeaway: Éxito = success. Salida = exit. Do not follow the wrong sign.

quizzes.question: You want to say a friend is sensible (level-headed). Which?
quizzes.why: Sensible in Spanish means sensitive — easily moved or hurt. Level-headed is sensato. So es muy sensible says your friend cries at adverts, which may not be the compliment you were reaching for.
quizzes.takeaway: Sensible = sensitive. Sensato = sensible.

quizzes.question: You want to say "actually, I live in Valencia". Which?
quizzes.why: Actualmente means currently, at present. For the English “actually” — correcting an assumption — Spanish uses en realidad or de hecho. Both are useful; they just are not the same word.
quizzes.takeaway: Actualmente = currently. En realidad = actually.

quizzes.place: a shop, holding up a shirt
quizzes.question: The shirt is too big. Which do you say?
quizzes.why: Largo means long — a long film, long hair, a long street. Big is grande. So es muy largo tells the assistant the shirt reaches your knees, not that it is too wide.
quizzes.takeaway: Largo = long. Grande = big.

quizzes.question: Which word means "clothes"?
quizzes.why: La ropa is clothes, and it is singular in Spanish even though English treats clothes as plural: la ropa está sucia, the clothes are dirty. Rope is la cuerda.
quizzes.takeaway: La ropa está — singular, always.

quizzes.question: The gestor asks for "la carpeta". What do they want?
quizzes.why: Carpeta is a folder or file — the thing your NIE paperwork lives in. A carpet is una alfombra, and a car park is un parking or un aparcamiento.
quizzes.takeaway: Carpeta = folder. Alfombra = carpet.

quizzes.question: The notice says "se ruega asistir". What is being asked?
quizzes.why: Asistir a means to attend — a meeting, a class, an event. To assist someone is ayudar. You will meet this one on every comunidad de vecinos notice in your building.
quizzes.takeaway: Asistir = attend. Ayudar = help.

quizzes.place: a form asking what you did
quizzes.question: You want to say "I realized I was wrong". Which?
options: Me di cuenta de que estaba equivocado.
quizzes.answer: Me di cuenta de que estaba equivocado.
quizzes.why: Realizar means to carry out or perform — realizar un trámite, to do a piece of paperwork. To realise something is darse cuenta de. Note the de: me di cuenta de que…
quizzes.takeaway: Realizar = carry out. Darse cuenta de = realise.

quizzes.question: You want to say "sorry to bother you". Which?
quizzes.why: Molestar simply means to bother or disturb — it carries none of the weight of the English word that looks like it. ¿Te molesta si…? is “do you mind if…”, and no molestar is what hangs on a hotel door.
quizzes.takeaway: Molestar = to bother. Completely ordinary, use it freely.

quizzes.question: You want to call a situation embarrassing. Which?
quizzes.why: Embarazoso/a does mean embarrassing — but only for situations and things, never for people. A person feels it: me dio vergüenza. And embarazada still means pregnant.
quizzes.takeaway: Situación embarazosa = fine. Estoy embarazada = a very different sentence.

quizzes.place: a phone shop, explaining a fault
quizzes.question: You want to say “the problem”. Which is correct?
quizzes.why: A group of nouns ending in -ma came from Greek and stayed masculine: el problema, el tema, el sistema, el idioma, el clima. They look feminine and are not.
quizzes.takeaway: El problema, el tema, el idioma. Greek words keep their gender.

quizzes.situationEn: A noun that breaks the rule
quizzes.question: You hurt your right hand and need to say so. Which is correct?
quizzes.why: Mano ends in -o but is feminine, so everything around it is feminine too: la mano derecha, las manos frías. Its friends in this club are la foto and la moto, both shortened from longer feminine words.
quizzes.takeaway: La mano, la foto, la moto. The -o is lying to you.

quizzes.situationEn: A noun that breaks it the other way
quizzes.place: wishing someone well in the morning
quizzes.question: It is nine in the morning and you pass a neighbour. Which greeting?
quizzes.why: Día ends in -a but is masculine, so the greeting is buenos días. The other two are feminine and behave normally: buenas tardes, buenas noches. That is why the first one looks odd next to the others.
quizzes.takeaway: Buenos días, buenas tardes, buenas noches. Only the first is masculine.

quizzes.place: a market stall, praising the produce
quizzes.question: The oranges on the stall are delicious. Which is correct?
quizzes.why: Everything lines up with the noun: plural feminine noun → plural verb (están) → plural feminine adjective (ricas). English changes almost nothing, so this is the habit that takes longest to build.
quizzes.takeaway: Noun sets the gender and number. Verb and adjective follow.

quizzes.question: You want to say "I am going to look for a flat". Which?
quizzes.why: Ir a + infinitive is how Spanish does the near future, and the a is compulsory — you cannot drop it the way English drops “to”. This one construction will carry most of your future tense for months.
quizzes.takeaway: Voy a + infinitive. Never leave out the a.

quizzes.question: You want to say "I have just arrived". Which?
quizzes.why: Acabar de + infinitive means to have just done something: acabo de comer, acaba de salir. It stays in the present tense even though English uses “have just”, and the verb after de stays in the infinitive.
quizzes.takeaway: Acabo de + infinitive = I have just…

quizzes.question: You are asking whether there is a pharmacy nearby. Which?
quizzes.why: Hay states that something exists, and it goes with un/una or no article at all. Está locates something you have both already identified: ¿Dónde está la farmacia? — the one we both know about.
quizzes.takeaway: Hay = there is one somewhere. Está = where the known one is.

quizzes.question: You want to say you can drive. Which?
quizzes.why: For a learned skill, Spanish uses saber + infinitive: sé conducir, sé cocinar, sé nadar. Puedo conducir is also grammatical but means you are able to right now — you have the car and you are not over the limit.
quizzes.takeaway: Sé = I know how to. Puedo = I am able to right now.

quizzes.place: a bar, needing one more thing
quizzes.question: You want to ask for the bill. Which verb?
options: Voy a preguntar por la cuenta.
quizzes.why: Pedir is to ask for a thing — the bill, a coffee, a favour. Preguntar is to ask a question. English uses “ask” for both, which is why this error survives so long.
quizzes.takeaway: Pedir = request a thing. Preguntar = ask a question.

quizzes.question: They say "trae algo de postre". What are they asking?
quizzes.why: Traer moves something towards where the speaker is; llevar moves it away. So trae el postre means bring it to me, and lleva el postre means take it with you somewhere else.
quizzes.takeaway: Traer = towards me. Llevar = away from me.

quizzes.question: It is three o clock. Which?
quizzes.why: The verb agrees with the hour, which is plural from two onwards: son las tres, son las diez. Only one o'clock is singular: es la una. Spain also runs on the 24-hour clock for timetables.
quizzes.takeaway: Es la una, but son las dos, las tres, las diez.

quizzes.question: You want to say "I get up at seven". Which?
quizzes.why: Levantarse is reflexive — you raise yourself — so the pronoun is compulsory: me levanto, te levantas. Without it, levanto means you lift something else. The a before a time is compulsory too.
quizzes.takeaway: Me levanto, me ducho, me acuesto. Keep the pronoun.

quizzes.question: The natural way to say "I forgot the keys" is:
quizzes.why: Spanish likes to present accidents as things that happened to you: literally “the keys got forgotten on me”. Because las llaves is the subject, the verb is plural — olvidaron. Olvidé las llaves is correct but sounds more deliberate.
quizzes.takeaway: Se me olvidó / se me olvidaron. The object decides the verb.

quizzes.question: You ate at a new place earlier today. In Spain you would most likely say:
options: Hoy comí en un sitio nuevo.
Hoy he comido en un sitio nuevo.
Hoy como en un sitio nuevo.
quizzes.answer: Hoy he comido en un sitio nuevo.
quizzes.why: For something finished but inside a period that is still going — today, this week, this year — Spain strongly prefers the pretérito perfecto: he comido, he ido, he visto. Much of Latin America uses the simple past here instead.
quizzes.takeaway: Hoy / esta semana / este año → he + participle.

quizzes.place: texting a friend who is ill
quizzes.question: You want to say "I hope you are well". Which?
quizzes.why: Espero que expresses a wish, not a fact, so what follows goes into the subjunctive: estés, not estás. You do not need to understand the whole system to use the handful that come up daily — this one, ojalá que, and quiero que.
quizzes.takeaway: Espero que + subjunctive. Learn it as a phrase first, a rule later.

quizzes.question: A friend says "¿qué tal, tío?". What did they call you?
quizzes.why: Tío/tía literally means uncle and aunt, but among friends in Spain it is simply mate or dude — and it is extremely common. It is informal: use it with friends, not with the clerk at the town hall.
quizzes.takeaway: Tío = mate, between friends. Never at the counter.

quizzes.situationEn: The word you will hear most
quizzes.question: What does "vale" mean in everyday Spain?
quizzes.why: Vale is the Spanish “OK” — agreement, acknowledgement, end of discussion. It comes from valer, to be worth, and it appears several times in almost every conversation. ¿Vale? at the end of a sentence is “alright?”.
quizzes.takeaway: Vale is the single most useful word in Spain. Use it liberally.

quizzes.question: A friend gets the flat they wanted. You say:
quizzes.why: Guay means cool or great, spelled exactly that way. It is casual and very Spanish — Latin America has its own words for this. Its close relative is ¡qué bien!, which works everywhere and with anyone.
quizzes.takeaway: Guay = cool. Qué bien = great, and safe in any country.

quizzes.question: In Spain, what do you call a mobile phone?
quizzes.why: Spain says el móvil; most of Latin America says el celular. Same story elsewhere in the shop: Spain uses el ordenador where others say la computadora. Both are correct Spanish — they are just from different places.
quizzes.takeaway: Móvil and ordenador in Spain. Celular and computadora elsewhere.

quizzes.place: a café at nine in the morning
quizzes.question: You want orange juice in Madrid. Which?
quizzes.why: Spain says zumo; Latin America says jugo. The same split runs through the menu: patatas in Spain, papas elsewhere. Order a jugo in Madrid and you will be understood, just placed instantly as a foreigner.
quizzes.takeaway: Zumo and patatas in Spain. Jugo and papas across the Atlantic.

quizzes.place: looking for somewhere to leave the car
quizzes.question: In Spain, how do you say "to park"?
quizzes.why: Spain uses aparcar, and the noun is el aparcamiento or simply el parking. Latin America prefers estacionar or parquear. Same for driving: Spain conducir, elsewhere manejar.
quizzes.takeaway: Aparcar and conducir in Spain.

quizzes.place: a bar on a Friday evening
quizzes.question: A friend says "mañana curro". What are they doing tomorrow?
quizzes.why: Currar is colloquial Spanish for working, and el curro is the job itself — voy al curro. It is informal and warm, not rude. The neutral word is trabajar, which you would use on any form.
quizzes.takeaway: Curro = job, informally. Trabajo on the paperwork.

quizzes.place: a small shop with a brown and yellow sign
quizzes.question: Where do you buy stamps in Spain?
quizzes.why: El estanco is a state-licensed tobacconist, and it is where you buy sellos (stamps) as well as bus passes and official paper. Correos does sell stamps too, but the estanco is nearer and has no queue.
quizzes.takeaway: Sellos at the estanco. It is the errand nobody explains.

quizzes.question: Your tap is dripping. Which shop?
quizzes.why: Ferretería is the hardware shop. The -ería ending marks the place where a thing is sold or done, and once you see it you can decode half a Spanish street: panadería bread, papelería stationery, peluquería hair, lavandería laundry.
quizzes.takeaway: -ería = the shop for that thing. One ending, twenty shops.

quizzes.place: your local health centre, on the phone
quizzes.question: You want to book an appointment with your GP. Which?
options: Quiero pedir cita con mi médico de cabecera.
Quiero preguntar cita con mi médico principal.
Quiero una reserva con mi doctor.
quizzes.answer: Quiero pedir cita con mi médico de cabecera.
quizzes.why: You pedir a cita, never preguntar one, and reserva is for restaurants and hotels. Your assigned GP is the médico de cabecera — the phrase the receptionist will use and expect back.
quizzes.takeaway: Pedir cita con el médico de cabecera. Three words that unlock the system.

quizzes.place: a notice in your building's hallway
quizzes.question: A notice announces "la junta de la comunidad". What is it?
quizzes.why: La comunidad de vecinos is the residents' association every block of flats has, and la junta is its meeting, where the lift repairs and the roof get argued about. If you rent, you usually do not pay the fees; if you buy, you do.
quizzes.takeaway: La junta = the meeting. Attend one and your Spanish will age five years in a night.

quizzes.place: the bin area at ten at night
quizzes.question: Which bin does glass go in?
quizzes.why: Spanish recycling runs on colour: verde glass, amarillo plastic and cans, azul paper and card, marrón organic, grey for the rest. Getting it wrong is the fastest way to meet your neighbours.
quizzes.takeaway: Verde glass, amarillo plastic, azul paper. Learn the colours, not the words.

quizzes.place: an empty flat with no power
quizzes.question: You need to set up an electricity contract. The phrase is:
quizzes.why: Dar de alta means to register or activate a service; dar de baja is to cancel it. You will use both constantly — for electricity, water, the gym, the phone. Mixing them up cancels the thing you were trying to start.
quizzes.takeaway: Alta = switch on. Baja = switch off. Opposites, one letter apart in your memory.

quizzes.place: an office full of filing cabinets
quizzes.question: What does a "gestor" do for you?
quizzes.why: A gestor — working from a gestoría — is a paid specialist who files your paperwork with the Spanish state: taxes, self-employment, residency, car transfers. There is no exact British or American equivalent, and almost every foreigner ends up using one.
quizzes.takeaway: Gestoría: the shortcut through Spanish bureaucracy. Budget for it.

quizzes.question: What does "autónomo" mean in Spain?
quizzes.why: Autónomo is the official status for the self-employed, with its own monthly social security payment — la cuota de autónomos — which is due whether you earned anything that month or not. If you freelance here, this word will run your year.
quizzes.takeaway: Autónomo = self-employed, and it costs a fixed monthly amount.

quizzes.question: How is "hola" pronounced?
quizzes.why: Spanish h is always silent: hola, hora, hospital, hermano. The sound English speakers reach for lives in the letter j instead. The h is still written, and leaving it out is a spelling error.
quizzes.takeaway: Write the h. Never say it.

quizzes.question: How is the j in "trabajo" pronounced?
options: Like the ch in Scottish loch
quizzes.answer: Like the ch in Scottish loch
quizzes.why: Spanish j is a rasp at the back of the throat — trabajo, jamón, hijo. The letter g does the same before e and i: gente, girar. Elsewhere g is hard, as in gato.
quizzes.takeaway: J always rasps. G rasps before e and i only.

quizzes.question: Which means "dog"?
quizzes.why: A single r between vowels is a quick tap; a double rr is a full trill. They are different words, not different accents: pero but, perro dog; caro expensive, carro cart. An r at the start of a word trills anyway.
quizzes.takeaway: Pero / perro, caro / carro. The trill carries meaning.

quizzes.place: ordering at a bar in Madrid
quizzes.question: In most of Spain, how is the c in "cerveza" pronounced?
quizzes.why: In most of Spain, c before e or i, and z anywhere, are pronounced like the English th in “think” — so cerveza is roughly ther-VE-tha. Southern Spain and all of Latin America use an s sound instead. Both are standard.
quizzes.takeaway: Central and northern Spain: c and z are th. Nobody will misunderstand either way.

quizzes.situationEn: When the accent changes the word
quizzes.question: What is the difference between "papa" and "papá"?
quizzes.why: The written accent marks which syllable is stressed, and moving it makes a different word: papa potato, papá dad; tu your, tú you; si if, sí yes; el the, él he. It is never optional.
quizzes.takeaway: The accent is not decoration. It is spelling.

quizzes.situationEn: The letter English does not have
quizzes.place: talking about how old you are
quizzes.question: What is the difference between "año" and "ano"?
options: One is a year, the other is not something you want to say
quizzes.answer: One is a year, the other is not something you want to say
quizzes.why: ñ is its own letter with its own sound, roughly the ny in “canyon”. Año is year; ano is the anatomical word. Saying how many anos you have is the classic first-week mistake.
quizzes.takeaway: Tengo treinta años. Always type the ñ.

quizzes.place: saying a word you have only read
quizzes.question: Where is the stress in "hablo" (no written accent)?
quizzes.why: Words ending in a vowel, n or s are stressed on the second-to-last syllable: HA-blo, CA-sa, ha-BLA-mos. Everything else is stressed on the last. A written accent exists precisely to mark the exceptions — ha-BLÓ, he spoke.
quizzes.takeaway: Vowel, n or s → stress the second-to-last. Otherwise the last.

quizzes.question: The stallholder says "son dos con cincuenta". How much?
quizzes.why: Prices are said as euros con céntimos: dos con cincuenta is €2.50. In writing, Spain uses a comma for the decimal and a dot for thousands — 1.250,50 € — which is the exact reverse of English, and the euro sign goes after the number.
quizzes.takeaway: Dos con cincuenta = 2,50 €. Comma for decimals, symbol at the end.

quizzes.question: A form is dated 04/09/2026. Which date is that?
quizzes.why: Spain writes dates day first: 04/09/2026 is the fourth of September. Said aloud it is el cuatro de septiembre, with de and no capital letter on the month. Getting this wrong on a cita previa costs you the appointment.
quizzes.takeaway: Day, month, year. And months are lower-case.

quizzes.question: Your appointment says 16:30. What time is that?
quizzes.why: Official Spain runs on the 24-hour clock — trains, appointments, opening hours. Spoken aloud people usually revert to twelve: las cuatro y media. And y media is half past, while menos cuarto is quarter to.
quizzes.takeaway: 16:30 written, “las cuatro y media” spoken.

quizzes.question: Which sounds most natural at a busy bar in Spain?
options: Perdone, señor, ¿sería tan amable de ponerme una caña?
quizzes.why: Spanish politeness lives in tone more than in extra words. A short, warm una caña, por favor is perfectly courteous; the long version sounds strained, and English speakers often over-pad because dropping “could I possibly” feels rude to them. It is not.
quizzes.takeaway: Short is not rude in Spain. Warm tone does the work.

quizzes.place: a shop where the assistant is your age
quizzes.question: Someone says "puedes tutearme". What are they offering?
options: Call me by my first name
quizzes.why: Tutear means to address someone as tú. Being invited to do it is a small social gift — take it immediately, because carrying on with usted after that reads as keeping your distance.
quizzes.takeaway: If they offer tutearme, switch on the spot.

quizzes.question: You need to squeeze past someone. Which?
quizzes.why: Perdón (or perdona/perdone) is the light one — excuse me, getting past, small interruptions. Lo siento carries real regret and is for things that actually went wrong. Using lo siento to get off the metro sounds oddly heavy.
quizzes.takeaway: Perdón to get past. Lo siento when you mean it.

quizzes.question: Someone thanks you. Which reply is most common in Spain?
quizzes.why: De nada is the standard “you're welcome”. Nada, nada and no hay de qué both work too. Bienvenido means welcome as in welcome to my home — it is not a reply to thanks, which is a direct import from English.
quizzes.takeaway: De nada. Never bienvenido.

quizzes.situationEn: Saying you did not catch it
quizzes.question: You did not catch what someone said. The most useful phrase is:
quizzes.why: This is the single most valuable sentence you can carry, because it keeps the conversation in Spanish instead of ending it. No hablo español closes the door — and after a few weeks it is not even true. ¿Perdón? just gets the same speed again.
quizzes.takeaway: Ask for slower, not for English. It is the whole difference.

quizzes.question: You need a word you do not know. Which?
quizzes.why: ¿Cómo se dice… en español? is the phrase that lets you build vocabulary from inside a conversation rather than from a list afterwards. Its partner is ¿Qué significa…? for when you hear something you do not know.
quizzes.takeaway: ¿Cómo se dice…? and ¿Qué significa…? Two phrases, endless vocabulary.

quizzes.place: someone asks how your Spanish is
quizzes.question: Someone asks how your Spanish is going. A natural modest answer:
quizzes.why: Más o menos — more or less — is the universal Spanish hedge, for your Spanish, the weather, the food and how you slept. Mucho bien is not Spanish: bien is an adverb, so it takes muy, giving muy bien.
quizzes.takeaway: Más o menos for honest. Muy bien, never mucho bien.

quizzes.place: a call you have been putting off
quizzes.question: You answer the phone in Spain. What do you say?
quizzes.why: ¿Dígame? — literally “tell me” — is the standard way to answer a phone in Spain, along with ¿sí?. ¿Quién es? sounds blunt, closer to “who is this”. Phone calls are where your Spanish feels worst, because you lose every visual clue.
quizzes.takeaway: ¿Dígame? to answer. And phone Spanish is hard for everyone.

quizzes.question: The shirt fits you well. Which?
quizzes.why: Quedar used this way works like gustar: the garment is the subject, so it is me queda bien for one item and me quedan bien for trousers or shoes. Me quedo means “I stay”, which is a different verb entirely.
quizzes.takeaway: Me queda bien = it suits me. Me quedo = I stay.

quizzes.place: the end of almost any transaction
quizzes.question: The assistant finishes and says "ya está". What do they mean?
options: That is it, we are done
quizzes.answer: That is it, we are done
quizzes.why: Ya está closes things — the payment went through, the form is filed, the haircut is finished. Ya on its own is one of the hardest little words in Spanish, sliding between already, now, and right away depending on where it sits.
quizzes.takeaway: Ya está = done. You will hear it ten times a day.
